draft.title: Bicameral structure of parliament
card: A bicameral parliament has two houses. The federal parliament has the House of Representatives (lower house) and the Senate (upper house). Victoria's parliament has the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council.
A bill must pass both houses before it can become law. Each house can debate it, change it or vote it down.
If the government does not control the upper house, the upper house may block a bill or amend it. This can slow or change the government's plans.
If the government does control the upper house, bills may pass with little review. Scrutiny of the bill is then weaker.
draft.remember: Two houses share the work. Who controls the upper house affects how closely a bill is checked.

a.q: Why does having two houses affect how laws are made?
opts: A bill needs both houses to pass it, so each can check it
A bill needs only the house the government controls
Only the upper house can debate and change a bill
The lower house passes bills and the upper house cannot vote
a.why: A bill must pass both houses, so each house can debate, amend or reject it. The tempting option that only the government's house matters is wrong, because the other house can still block a bill.
a.clue: Think about what must happen before a bill becomes law.

b.q: A state government has a majority in its lower house but not in its upper house. It introduces a controversial bill. What is the most likely effect?
opts: The upper house may amend or reject it, delaying the plan
The bill becomes law because the lower house has passed it
The bill is checked less because the government is in power
The upper house must pass it because the lower house has
b.why: The government lacks control of the upper house, so that house may amend, delay or reject the bill. Passing the lower house is not enough, because both houses must pass a bill.
b.clue: Which house does the government not control?

a.best: A bill needs both houses to pass it, so each can check it

b.best: The upper house may amend or reject it, delaying the plan
